tldr: This paper proposes GraspMeanFlow, an SE(3)-equivariant MeanFlow framework that generates high-precision 6-DoF grasp poses in just a few network evaluation steps while preserving SE(3)-equivariance with respect to object point clouds, significantly outperforming existing methods in both speed and success rate.
hero_caption: Overall framework overview of GraspMeanFlow. Given an object point cloud, a grasp pose sampled from a prior, and a time pair $(s, t)$, an SE(3)-equivariant network predicts the average velocity over a finite interval. This enables accurate grasp pose generation with very few steps using an Euler sampler or an exp-SO(3) sampler.
overview:
In robotic manipulation, generating diverse and accurate 6-DoF grasp poses from observed object point clouds is crucial. Recently, SE(3)-equivariant flow-based models (such as EquiGraspFlow) have emerged. They generate poses that transform consistently with object rotations and translations. However, because they sample by numerically integrating ordinary differential equations, they require tens of number of function evaluations (NFEs) per grasp. This forms a major bottleneck for real-time manipulation.

To solve this, the authors propose GraspMeanFlow. It extends MeanFlow—a popular fast generation framework in Euclidean space that directly learns the average velocity over a finite time interval—to the SE(3) manifold. To handle the non-commutativity of the rotation group $\mathrm{SO}(3)$, the average velocity is defined using the time-ordered exponential, exactly reproducing the rigid-body displacement accumulated over the interval. In addition, the authors introduce a conditioning architecture that accepts time pairs $(s, t)$ without breaking equivariance, as well as a semigroup loss that avoids numerically unstable differential identities.

Experiments on the ACRONYM dataset demonstrate that a single function evaluation (NFE 1) of GraspMeanFlow reaches the distribution fidelity (EMD) that conventional flow models require five steps to approach. Furthermore, it improves grasp success rate by up to 24.3 points in the 5-step regime while generating grasp distributions that transform exactly with the object.
contributions: Formulating the average velocity via the time-ordered exponential to exactly reproduce rigid-body displacements on the non-commutative SE(3) manifold, and providing theoretical proof that equivariance is preserved under few-step sampling.
Proposing a time-embedding mechanism that conditions the Vector Neuron backbone on a time pair $(s, t)$ while preserving SO(3)-equivariance with virtually no added parameters.

Presenting two complementary training losses: a semigroup loss (GMF-SG) that completely bypasses Jacobian-vector products (JVPs) for stable training, and a differential identity loss combined with optimal transport coupling (GMF-JVP).
Achieving an improvement in grasp success rate of up to 24.3 points over existing baselines in the few-step regime (NFE 5) on the ACRONYM benchmark.

sections.heading: Equivariant flows in few steps: tackling MeanFlow on SE(3)
sections.summary: SE(3)-equivariant flow models offer high rotational robustness for 6-DoF grasp generation from point clouds, but sampling requires dozens of integration steps. This paper extends MeanFlow to SE(3) to predict average velocities over finite intervals, enabling few-step generation while preserving equivariance.
sections.details:
Generating 6-DoF parallel-jaw grasp poses $T=(R, x) \in \mathrm{SE}(3)$ from 3D point clouds is formulated as conditional generative modeling because successful grasps are multi-modal. Recently, EquiGraspFlow showed excellent performance by building SE(3)-equivariance directly into the model architecture, allowing it to track object rotations and translations without data augmentation.

However, the primary bottleneck of such flow and diffusion models is sampling speed. Because they numerically integrate continuous-time velocity fields, generating a single grasp requires tens of network evaluations (e.g., 80 evaluations using 4th-order Runge-Kutta in EquiGraspFlow). In real-world manipulation, robots need to generate and evaluate hundreds of candidates instantaneously whenever the scene changes. Ideally, we want to sample an equivalent grasp distribution in one or just a few steps.

MeanFlow offers a promising direction by directly predicting the average velocity over a finite interval rather than instantaneous velocities. However, grasp poses live in SE(3), where the rotation group $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is non-commutative. Integrating velocities naively as in Euclidean space does not yield the endpoint pose. Flattening the pose into Euclidean representations destroys the manifold's geometric structure and equivariance.

In this work, the authors define average velocity on SE(3) using the time-ordered exponential and develop GraspMeanFlow for point-cloud-conditioned equivariant generation. This enables high-quality grasp pose generation in only a few steps without increasing model capacity.

sections.heading: SE(3) fundamentals, Flow Matching, and Euclidean MeanFlow
sections.summary: This section reviews rigid-body kinematics in SE(3) and flow matching for grasp pose generation. It also recaps the core identity of MeanFlow in Euclidean space, which learns average velocities over finite intervals.
sections.details:
The rigid-body transformation group $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ consists of a rotation matrix $R \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$ and a translation vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^3$. Using angular velocity $\omega \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and linear velocity $v \in \mathbb{R}^3$, the trajectory of a rigid pose in the spatial frame is given by $\dot{R} = [\omega] R$ and $\dot{x} = v$, where $[\cdot]$ maps a 3D vector to a skew-symmetric matrix (corresponding to the cross product).

In flow matching for 6-DoF grasp generation, a probability path is designed from a simple prior (Gaussian centered at the point cloud centroid and uniform rotations) to the ground-truth grasp distribution. The network learns the instantaneous velocity field $(\omega_\theta, v_\theta)$ at intermediate time $t$. At inference time, numerical integration is performed from $t=1$ to $t=0$.

In contrast, MeanFlow models the average velocity $u(s, t, z_t) = \frac{1}{t-s} \int_s^t v_\tau d\tau$ over the interval $[s, t]$. Differentiating this with respect to $t$ yields the MeanFlow identity connecting average velocity and instantaneous velocity, which serves as a regression target using Jacobian-vector products (JVPs). This paper extends this formulation to the non-commutative Lie group SE(3).

sections.heading: Defining and learning SE(3) average velocity equivariantly
sections.summary: The authors define SE(3) average velocity via the time-ordered exponential to handle non-commutative rotations, and prove distribution invariance under equivariant flow maps. They present two training objectives: a JVP-free semigroup loss and a JVP-based differential identity loss.
sections.details:
The core ideas and designs of GraspMeanFlow are as follows:

- **Formulating Average Velocity on SE(3)**: The average velocity $(\omega^{\mathrm{avg}}, v^{\mathrm{avg}})$ over $[s, t]$ is defined as a Lie algebra element that reproduces the rigid displacement over the interval in a single step. For rotations, it uses the time-ordered matrix exponential $\mathcal{T}\!\exp$ to handle non-commutativity: $R_t R_s^\top = \exp((t-s)[\omega^{\mathrm{avg}}])$.
- **Differential Identity and its Challenge**: Differentiating this with respect to $t$ yields a differential identity involving the left Jacobian $J$ of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. However, JVP-based objectives can be numerically unstable on rotation groups.
- **JVP-Free Training with Semigroup Loss**: The authors exploit the associative property of group multiplication, $D(s, t) = D(m, t) D(s, m)$. By enforcing that a two-step composition via an intermediate time $m$ matches the direct one-step prediction over $[s, t]$, the model trains stably without computing Jacobians $J$ or JVPs.
- **Warmup with $\alpha$-Flow**: To stabilize early training, the model pre-trains on an $\alpha$-Flow loss using ground-truth velocities from the data before gradually transitioning to the semigroup loss.
- **Preserving SE(3)-Equivariance**: Time pairs $(s, t)$ are fed into the network by multiplying time scalars with an equivariant vector direction $d$ from the Vector Neuron backbone. This completely preserves architecture equivariance. Furthermore, the paper rigorously proves in terms of pushforward measures that transportation by an equivariant average-velocity field preserves distribution invariance.
- **Inference Samplers**: In addition to standard Euler integration, the authors introduce an 'exp-SO(3) sampler' that estimates the endpoint pose from the predicted average velocity and updates rotation along the geodesic.

captions.F1: GraspMeanFlow architecture and sampling flow. Given a point cloud $\mathcal{P}$, current pose $T_t$, and time pair $(s, t)$, the equivariant network predicts the average velocity to update toward the target pose in few steps.

sections.heading: ACRONYM benchmark results: high grasp success in few steps
sections.summary: Evaluation across four ACRONYM categories (Bowl, Laptop, Mug, Pencil) shows that a 1-step generation achieves distribution fidelity matching a 5-step baseline. In 5-step generation, it outperforms EquiGraspFlow by up to 24.3 points in grasp success rate.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted on four ACRONYM categories using the same point cloud encoder (VN-DGCNN) and training budget (~7 hours). Baselines include EquiGraspFlow (equivariant CNF), SE(3)-DiffusionFields (diffusion model), and BRIDGER (stochastic interpolant bridge). The authors evaluate two proposed variants: 'GMF-SG' (semigroup loss + independent coupling) and 'GMF-JVP' (differential identity + per-object optimal transport coupling).

- **Distribution Fidelity (EMD)**: At a single evaluation step (NFE 1), GMF-SG achieves an EMD of 0.418. This matches what EquiGraspFlow achieves after nearly 5 steps (0.416), while EquiGraspFlow fails completely at NFE 1 (0.734).
- **Simulation Grasp Success Rate (Isaac Gym)**: In the practical few-step regime (NFE 5), GMF-JVP demonstrates strong performance. It improves success rate over EquiGraspFlow by +24.3 points on Laptop, +21.7 points on Bowl, +12.8 points on Pencil, and +3.0 points on Mug. At NFE 10, it averages 96.3% across the four categories, significantly higher than the baseline's 91.2%.
- **Inference Latency**: GMF-SG reaches an EMD of 0.418 at NFE 1 in just 31.5 ms. GMF-JVP achieves a 96.3% success rate at NFE 5 in 56.3 ms, which is orders of magnitude faster than SE(3)-DiffusionFields (1338.7 ms for 96.1% success).
- **Ablations and Analysis**: For the differential identity, using the spatial frame is essential; formulating it in the body frame causes training divergence on symmetric objects (Bowl). Additionally, self-consistency loss must be paired with boundary anchor loss.

captions.F4: Simulation results of generated grasps at NFE 5 across categories (green: success, red: failure). The proposed methods (GMF-SG and GMF-JVP, red box on the center-right) show significantly fewer failures (red) and generate stable poses compared to baselines (left three columns).

sections.heading: Why it works, and remaining open challenges
sections.summary: The benefits of average-velocity modeling concentrate in the few-step regime, where interval averaging absorbs numerical integration errors. Remaining challenges include geometric mismatches on objects with continuous rotational symmetry (Pencil) and sampler schedule optimization.
sections.details:
As the results show, the strength of the average velocity model is maximized in the low-NFE regime. At high NFEs such as 20, conventional flow models that accumulate instantaneous velocities converge sufficiently, narrowing the performance gap. However, at low computational budgets like NFE 5, predicting interval averages directly reduces integration error dramatically.

Two primary limitations are discussed:

- **Axially Symmetric Objects (Pencil)**: For objects with continuous rotational symmetry along an axis, physically equivalent grasps are penalized as large displacements by the Lie algebra logarithmic map (log). A target formulation accounting for the object's symmetry group by measuring distance to the minimal representative is needed.
- **Sampler Schedules and Negative Results**: While the endpoint-predicting exp-SO(3) sampler is highly effective at NFE 5 and above, relying heavily on predicted endpoints at NFE 1–2 leads to failures. Furthermore, post-training the model on self-generated successful grasps (ReFlow) improved Euler integration, but yielded a negative result by degrading the endpoint-prediction sampler's accuracy.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.summary: The paper establishes SE(3)-equivariant MeanFlow by accurately reproducing rigid displacements, achieving few-step 6-DoF grasp generation. Balancing inference speed and grasp success without increasing model capacity represents an important step forward for real-time robot manipulation.
sections.details: This work defines average velocity on the SE(3) manifold to exactly reproduce rigid-body displacements over finite time intervals, proposing the point-cloud-conditioned equivariant generative model GraspMeanFlow. The authors mathematically prove that equivariance is preserved and establish two complementary training methods: a JVP-free semigroup loss and a JVP-based differential loss with optimal transport. Comprehensive experiments on the ACRONYM dataset demonstrate that exceptionally high grasp success rates and accurate pose distributions can be obtained with just a few network evaluation steps.

sections.heading: Appendix: mathematical derivations, network details, and ReFlow negative results
sections.summary: The appendix details the derivation of the SE(3) left Jacobian, proofs for the semigroup property and Vector Neuron equivariance, and discusses why ReFlow on self-generated samples degraded performance for certain samplers.
sections.details:
The appendix provides theoretical and implementation details supporting the main text:

- **Mathematical Details on Left Jacobian and Semigroup**: Provides the step-by-step derivation of the left Jacobian $J(\phi)$ from the Fréchet derivative of the time-ordered matrix exponential (Wilcox formula) and a formal proof of the semigroup identity $D(s, t) = D(m, t) D(s, m)$ via group associativity.
- **Network Architecture and Equivariance Proof**: Explains how time scalars $t$ and interval durations $h=t-s$ are injected by multiplying shared equivariant direction vectors $d$, preserving full network equivariance with only 512 additional parameters.
- **Per-Object Optimal Transport (Per-Object OT)**: Instead of solving OT across the entire mini-batch, solving independent $J_i \times J_i$ linear assignment problems per object prevents distorting the marginal distribution of the conditional prior and reduces computational complexity from $O(n^3 J^3)$ to $O(n J^3)$.
- **Negative Results from ReFlow Fine-Tuning**: Running ReFlow post-training using simulator-verified grasps to straighten trajectories improved the Euler sampler, but degraded the endpoint-predicting exp-SO(3) sampler by blurring endpoint resolution.

takeaways: For MeanFlow on non-commutative manifolds (SO(3) or SE(3)), average velocity must be defined via displacement matching using time-ordered exponentials rather than naive velocity integration.
While differential identities with Jacobian-vector products (JVPs) can be unstable on manifolds, a semigroup consistency loss based on group associativity completely avoids JVPs for stable training.

In an equivariant Vector Neuron backbone, two time inputs can be injected by multiplying time scalars with shared equivariant direction vectors, preserving equivariance without increasing model capacity.

When applying optimal transport (OT) coupling to object-conditioned flow models, solving it per-object rather than across the full batch prevents prior distortion and significantly reduces computation.
limitations: On objects with rotational symmetry (e.g., pencils), geometric rotation differences between physically equivalent grasps are penalized as losses, capping performance.
At extremely small step budgets (NFE 1–2), the exp-SO(3) sampler makes excessive jumps toward predicted endpoints from the prior, causing grasp success rates to drop sharply.
Post-training on self-generated successful grasps (ReFlow) degrades endpoint prediction accuracy, leading to performance drops when using endpoint-dependent samplers.
